mcqs.question: A landing page renders a decorative flourish as with no alt attribute. A screen-reader user reports hearing the file path read out between the headline and the paragraph. Which change fixes it, and why?
options: Add alt="flourish": the graphic still needs a name in the accessibility tree, and a one-word name keeps the announcement short.

Add alt="" - present but empty: the HTML spec requires the empty string for a decorative image, and that empty value is the signal that keeps it out of the announcement. A missing alt is a different, unspecified case, which is exactly why the file path is being read.
Add role="img" and aria-label="": the empty accessible name is what removes the image from the accessibility tree.
Add title="Decorative flourish" instead of alt: title is the fallback name, and screen readers only use it for tooltips.
mcqs.explanation: Decorative means the image adds nothing a user needs, so its accessible name has to be the empty string: alt must be present and its value must be empty, the state the HTML spec defines for a purely decorative image (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/images.html#alt) and the one assistive technology skips (https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/decorative/). A missing alt is not the same statement: it is the unspecified case, where the browser or the screen reader has to guess and commonly falls back to the file name or to an unlabelled "graphic" - the report being described. The strongest distractor is option 0: naming the flourish does not make it decorative, it makes it an image that gets announced on every visit, so a one-word name only shortens the interruption. Option 2 fails for the same reason as no alt, with extra steps: an empty aria-label produces no name at all, and role="img" (already implied by the element) keeps the node in the tree as an unnamed graphic. Option 3 swaps one announced string for another - title becomes the accessible name or description and is still read. Two limits worth saying out loud: alt="" is only safe when nothing else depends on that image for a name, so never put it on the only content of a link or a button, and a flourish that belongs to the site-wide chrome is better moved to CSS as a decorative background, which the spec prefers over repeating identical decorative markup on every page.

mcqs.question: A teammate ships <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no"> because iOS zooms into a text input on focus and "it looks broken". What does that actually do, and what is the right fix?
options: It removes pinch-zoom wherever the hint is honoured - still the case in many Android browsers and embedded WebViews - so a low-vision user cannot enlarge the page; MDN warns about exactly this and WCAG 1.4.4 expects zoom up to 200%. Leave zoom alone and give form fields a font size of at least 16px, which is what stops the focus zoom.
Nothing lasting: iOS 10+ ignores user-scalable=no and maximum-scale by default, every other engine has followed, so the attribute is dead code with no user-visible effect.
It is an acceptable trade-off: desktop browser zoom keeps working, and a mobile user who needs magnification can use the operating system screen magnifier instead.
It only caps the starting zoom level: users can still pinch past it and text keeps reflowing, so the impact is cosmetic until the layout breaks.
mcqs.explanation: These two keys are hints about zoom, not switches the page owns. MDN documents that browser settings can ignore them and that iOS 10+ ignores them by default (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/meta/name/viewport), which means shipping them is a bet on the one engine that disobeys while every engine that obeys takes pinch-zoom away from the people who need it most; the same page carries a warning that disabling zoom prevents low-vision users from reading, and points at WCAG 1.4.4 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/resize-text.html). The real cause of the reported symptom is text size: mobile Safari zooms into a focused field whose font size is below 16px, so setting the field font size to 16px or more removes the zoom without touching the viewport at all. The strongest distractor is option 1, because it is a half-truth: iOS really does ignore user-scalable=no by default, but "can ignore" is not "must ignore", and many Android browsers and WebViews still honour the hint - relying on one engine behaviour means the accessibility bug appears on the devices of whatever share does not. Option 2 is wrong twice: an OS magnifier shows a magnified picture without reflowing anything and is not a substitute a page may assume, and desktop zoom does nothing for a phone. Option 3 confuses initial-scale (where zoom starts) with maximum-scale (the ceiling); the ceiling is the block, and the reflow argument belongs to text resizing, not to pinch-zoom.

mcqs.question: A page has three nav landmarks - header navigation, a breadcrumb, and footer navigation - and the screen-reader landmark list shows "navigation" three times. What actually makes them distinguishable?
options: Give each nav a distinct accessible name - aria-label="Primary", "Breadcrumb", "Footer", or aria-labelledby pointing at a visible heading - so each entry in the landmark list reads differently.
Nothing is needed: a nav inside footer inherits the contentinfo context, so it is already announced as the footer navigation; only the breadcrumb is ambiguous.
Add an h2 inside each nav: the heading sits inside the landmark, so it becomes the landmark's accessible name.
Point aria-describedby at a sentence inside each nav that explains its purpose: the description tells the three entries apart without duplicating visible text.
mcqs.explanation: A landmark gets its name from an accessible name, and the ARIA Authoring Practices are explicit: if a landmark role is used more than once, give each instance a unique label, using aria-labelledby when the area starts with a visible heading and aria-label when it does not (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/landmark-regions/). Nothing else changes what the landmark list says. The strongest distractor is option 1, because it borrows a real rule and applies it to the wrong element: header and footer map to banner and contentinfo only when they are page-level, and that mapping is about those elements, never about naming a nav nested inside them. A nav is navigation wherever it lives, so the footer one is a third "navigation" until you name it. Option 2 confuses proximity with naming: a heading inside a landmark does not name it, and only an explicit aria-labelledby reference does; adding headings improves heading-based navigation while the landmark list stays identical. Option 3 confuses description with name - aria-describedby supplies a description that may be read after the name, and every list that shows names still shows three identical entries. One more detail interviewers listen for: do not put the role in the label, because "Site navigation" is announced as "Site navigation navigation".

mcqs.question: A product-card image renders 320px wide on desktop and full-bleed on phones. The markup is . On a 1440px-wide viewport, what is wrong and what is the fix?
options: Nothing: after layout the browser measures the 320px card and fetches the matching candidate, so sizes only matters as a preload hint.
sizes describes a full-viewport slot, so the browser computes roughly 1440px and fetches a much larger file than the 320px card needs; state the real slot, e.g. sizes="(width <= 600px) 100vw, 320px".
Width descriptors in srcset must be ordered largest-first; otherwise the browser takes the first entry, here the 480w file.
Without x density descriptors the browser ignores srcset entirely and always downloads the src file.
mcqs.explanation: sizes is the declaration the browser uses to compute the rendered slot before it downloads anything, so 100vw tells it the image fills a 1440px viewport and it chooses a candidate for that width even though the card is 320px: the classic over-fetch. Declaring the real slot, with the last condition as the default, makes the selection match the layout (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Guides/Responsive_images). The strongest distractor is option 0: selection is driven by sizes, not by a post-layout measurement, which is precisely why the browser can start fetching early and why a wrong sizes keeps costing bytes. Option 3 confuses the implicit sizes fallback (100vw) with srcset being ignored, and x descriptors are for fixed-size slots rather than a requirement. Option 2 invents an ordering rule; the browser compares candidates by computed density, not by list position.

mcqs.question: A "your session expires in 60 seconds" prompt must block the page until the user answers. Which native construction actually does that?
options: A popover="manual" element: it stays open until explicitly dismissed, so it blocks interaction with the rest of the page.
A <dialog> element opened with show(), because opening a dialog is modal by definition.
A <dialog> element opened with showModal(): the rest of the page becomes inert, focus is kept inside, and Escape dismisses it.
A popover="auto" element plus aria-modal="true", so assistive technology treats the page as blocked.
mcqs.explanation: Modality comes from showModal(): it makes outside content inert, contains focus, renders a ::backdrop and supports Escape dismissal, which is exactly the must-answer-first requirement (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/dialog). The strongest distractor is option 0: manual only changes light-dismiss behavior (a manual popover does not close on outside clicks), but the Popover API is always non-modal, so the page stays fully interactive behind it. Option 1 uses show(), which opens non-modally with no backdrop and no inertness, and option 3 lies to assistive technology: aria-modal does not create inertness or focus containment, and an auto popover still light-dismisses on outside interaction (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API).

mcqs.question: A pricing table is written with <div> elements and CSS grid and matches the design pixel for pixel. What is lost for screen-reader users, and what is the right fix?
options: Only the visual affordances are missing; adding role="grid" to the wrapper is enough to expose it as a table.
Nothing structural: add tabindex="0" and an aria-label to every cell so users can tab through the values.

The divs expose no header-cell relationships, so figures are announced without their row and column context; use a native <table> with a <caption>, <th scope="col"> for the price columns and <th scope="row"> for the plan names.
Adding role="table" to the wrapper makes the browser infer rows and cells from the child divs.
mcqs.explanation: A native table is what creates the row and column header associations a screen reader announces while moving between cells, the caption names the table, and scope states each axis explicitly (https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/). The strongest distractor is option 3: ARIA roles do not cascade, so a role="table" wrapper with plain div children exposes no rows, cells or headers; you would need role="row", role="columnheader" and role="cell" on every element and would still be re-owning table navigation, which is strictly worse than the native element. Option 0's role="grid" is an interactive, focus-managed widget pattern with its own keyboard contract, not a shortcut for read-only data, and option 1 turns a many-cell table into a tab-stop maze while aria-label expresses no relationships.

mcqs.question: A form posts to /profile with method="post". Without JavaScript, the Save button must submit to /profile/save and the Delete button to /profile/delete. Which markup works?
options: Set formtarget="/profile/delete" on the Delete button.
Nest a second form, <form action="/profile/delete" method="post">, inside the existing form around the Delete button.
Set action="/profile/delete" directly on the Delete <button>.
Give each submit button a formaction override: <button type="submit" formaction="/profile/delete">, plus formmethod if the method must change too.
mcqs.explanation: formaction is the per-button override for the form's processing URL, and its siblings formmethod, formenctype and formtarget override the other navigation attributes, so one form can reach different endpoints with zero JavaScript (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#form-submission-algorithm). The strongest distractor is option 0: formtarget is a real override, but it chooses the browsing context (_self, _blank), not the URL, so the POST still lands on /profile. Option 1 is invalid HTML because forms cannot be nested, so the inner form is ignored, and option 2 invents an action attribute on <button>: the button-level attribute is formaction, not action.

scenarios.prompt: At 60rem and wider this page shows Filters in the left column with Results and Details stacked to their right. The DOM lists Results, Details, Filters. Accessibility review files three findings: a keyboard user tabs into "Result 1" before reaching the filter checkbox that scopes it; a screen-reader user hears the results and then the details before the filters; below 60rem everything reads in a sensible order. (a) Explain the mechanism behind the two findings and say which parts of the CSS are not at fault. (b) Give the fix that keeps both breakpoints looking the same. (c) List the "fixes" you would reject, and what you would verify before shipping.

code.code:
Result 1

Details

scenarios.modelAnswer:
(a) Predict the sequence first, because both audiences get the same one: the accessibility tree and the Tab order are built from the DOM, so they read Results, Details, Filters. At 60rem and up a screen-reader user hears "Result 1" and its link, then the details paragraph, then the checkbox that decides which results exist; a keyboard user lands on Result 1 first and only reaches the filter after the content it filters. Visually it is the reverse, so a sighted keyboard user also sees focus start on the right and jump back to the left edge, which gets reported as "focus jumps around". (b) The mechanism is that display: grid and grid-template-areas are paint-time placement: they move boxes, not nodes. Nothing in that stylesheet rewrites reading order or sequential focus, and the same is true of flex order, position: absolute and float. So the CSS is not lying - it does exactly what the source order allowed - and the bug is that the DOM order disagrees with the hierarchy the design expresses. The tell is to turn CSS off: the linearized page reads Results, Details, Filters, which is not a coherent document. The fix is one move: put the aside first in main and change nothing in the stylesheet, because placement is already declared per id through grid-area, so the visual result is identical at 60rem and the source order now matches the visual order:
Result 1

Details

Then handle the second breakpoint, which is where this fix can bite: below 60rem there is no template, items auto-place in source order, and the filters now come first on phones too. For a filterable list that is usually the right flow, but if the narrow design wants results first, that is a product decision to settle in the layout or the content - moving the filter panel into a disclosure that opens above the results, for example. What it is not is a reason to restore the old order with order or tabindex. If the grid had no explicit placement, reordering the source would move the desktop layout, and the fix would be to give each item an explicit grid-area so source order and visual order can be chosen independently. (c) Rejected fixes: positive tabindex (it creates a second ordering that only governs focus, has to be maintained by hand as content changes, and still leaves a screen-reader user reading results before filters); grid order (same class of trap, focus and reading order stay in DOM order); aria-flowto (no meaningful support); and shipping two DOMs with aria-hidden on one (duplicate ids, double maintenance, and a focus trap waiting to happen). Verification: tab through the page at both breakpoints, read it in document order with a screen reader, confirm the focus ring on the checkbox is visible, and confirm the new first element does not surprise anyone - if the filters now start the page, a heading on the aside gives the reader an anchor.
rubric: States that tab order and screen-reader reading order follow DOM source order and that grid placement (grid-area, grid-template-areas, order) is visual only.
Predicts both symptoms concretely: focus reaches Result 1 before the scoping filter, and linear reading announces results and details before filters.
Fixes it by moving the aside earlier in the source and notes the stylesheet needs no change because placement is per id.
Checks the sub-60rem layout after the reorder and treats a design conflict there as a product decision, not as a reason to keep the wrong DOM order.
Rejects positive tabindex / CSS order / aria-flowto with the reason (split ordering, no effect on reading order, maintenance) and names keyboard plus screen-reader verification at both breakpoints.

scenarios.prompt: This revenue table is built from divs and CSS grid so it matches the design. It looks correct, but a screen-reader user reports hearing "North 120k 135k South 98k 110k" with no idea which figure belongs to which quarter. (a) Name what is lost and why. (b) Rewrite the markup so the same visual result is accessible. (c) State what you would verify before shipping.

code.code:
Region
Q1
Q2
North
$120k
$135k
South
$98k
$110k

scenarios.modelAnswer:
(a) The divs are layout only: nothing in that markup exposes a table, a row, a cell or a header. The aria-label on the section names a region, not a table, so the accessibility tree holds a flat run of text. Two things are lost. First, header-cell associations: when focus reaches $135k there is no reason for the screen reader to say "Q2, North", and that context is exactly what a data table contributes. Second, table navigation: commands that move between cells or jump by row and column are unavailable, so a small grid becomes a linear read of numbers whose meaning depends on the visual position the user cannot see. (b) Use the native element for the semantics and keep the visuals in CSS:
Quarterly revenue by region
RegionQ1Q2
North$120k$135k
South$98k$110k
The caption names the table instead of assigning a name to a region, scope="col" states the column axis on the quarter headers and scope="row" states the row axis on the region names, and the figures stay in td. Reproduce the design with table CSS instead of going back to divs: table-layout: fixed plus a colgroup with column widths for the 2fr/1fr/1fr proportions, border-collapse for the rules, and padding and alignment for the cells. The point of the fix is to keep one source of truth: the element carries the relationships, the stylesheet carries the look. Do not paper over it with ARIA on divs either, because role="table" alone creates no rows, cells or headers, and building the full role set by hand means re-owning table navigation for no gain. (c) Verify with a real screen reader rather than only with an accessibility-tree inspector: confirm the table is announced with its caption and that each figure is announced together with its region and quarter. Then check the narrow viewport, where the table may need horizontal scrolling: the scrollable region has to be reachable and operable with the keyboard, and the visual result must still match the breakpoints the design specified. Finally, decide deliberately what happens on phones if the table is meant to collapse, instead of stripping the semantics to make it fit.
rubric: Identifies the root cause as missing table semantics (no rows, cells or header associations), not as a styling gap.
Rewrites with a native <table>, a <caption>, <th scope="col"> for the quarters and <th scope="row"> for the regions, with figures in <td>.
Keeps the visual result with table CSS (table-layout: fixed, colgroup widths, border-collapse, padding) instead of reverting to divs.
Rejects ARIA-only and tabindex fixes, explaining that role="table" does not cascade and a full row/cell/header role set would have to be hand-built.
Names concrete verification: screen-reader announcement of each cell with both headers, plus keyboard access and layout at narrow viewports.
